name: Loss Aversion
description: Losses loom psychologically larger than equivalent gains — people work harder to avoid losing something than to gain the equivalent.
design_relevance_note: Underlies 'don't lose your streak,' 'your cart will expire,' and loss-framed messaging generally.
myth_risk_note: The existence of loss aversion is well supported, but the popular 'losses hurt about twice as much as gains' figure is contested: Brown et al. 2024 give 1.955 [1.820, 2.102] while Walasek et al. 2024 give 1.31 [1.10, 1.53] and flag poor data quality. Scopes differ (all estimate types vs CPT lambda from mixed gambles).
prevalence_note: Core prospect-theory concept, taught in essentially every behavioral-design curriculum and constantly invoked in framing/messaging discussions.

findings.description: A direct multinational replication of Kahneman & Tversky's 1979 prospect-theory items (4,098 participants, 19 countries) reproduced 94% of items, with some attenuation; 12 of 13 theoretical contrasts replicated, 100% in some countries, with notable heterogeneity between countries and within individuals.
findings.effect_size: 94% of items replicated; 12 of 13 theoretical contrasts; n = 4,098, 19 countries
findings.source_title: Replicating patterns of prospect theory for decision under risk

findings.description: A standardized survey combining Hofstede cultural-dimension items with lottery-based loss-aversion measures, administered across 53 countries, found that the degree of loss aversion (not merely its presence) varies systematically with national culture: individualism, power distance, and masculinity are each positively associated with greater loss aversion, uncertainty avoidance shows a weaker relationship than predicted, and a country's distribution of major religions is also related to its measured loss aversion; the relationship between loss aversion and macroeconomic variables is comparatively much weaker than the cultural-variable relationships.
findings.source_title: The Impact of Culture on Loss Aversion

findings.description: Across 607 estimates from 150 articles (1992-2017) in several disciplines, the mean loss aversion coefficient is 1.955, with a 95 percent probability that the true value lies in [1.820, 2.102]; few observable study-design characteristics are substantially correlated with differences in estimates.
findings.source_title: Meta-analysis of Empirical Estimates of Loss Aversion

findings.description: People underweight merely-probable outcomes relative to certain ones (certainty effect) and discard components shared across choice options (isolation effect); the value function is concave for gains, convex for losses, and steeper for losses than gains (loss aversion); decision weights replace raw probabilities.
findings.source_title: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk

findings.description: Restricting to studies that fit the cumulative-prospect-theory lambda parameter to individual choices between mixed gambles, a random-effects meta-analysis finds a small lambda of 1.31 (95% CI 1.10-1.53), and the authors conclude that few suitable studies exist and much of the data are of poor quality, preventing precise parameter estimates.
findings.source_title: A meta-analysis of loss aversion in risky contexts

applications.title: A Uganda lab experiment shows paying tax makes citizens punish corrupt officials harder
applications.description: Political scientist Lucy Martin (UNC Chapel Hill), published via Innovations for Poverty Action, ran laboratory experiments in Uganda testing whether taxation -- by pushing loss-averse citizens below their reference point of already-earned income -- increases citizens' willingness to sanction non-accountable government officials. In a single-shot game, taxation increased citizens' willingness to punish leaders by 12% overall, and by 30% among the subgroup with the most real-world experience paying taxes. Follow-up experiments specifically isolated loss aversion (rather than a general sense of civic ownership) as the driving mechanism, and a separate survey experiment found the same pattern held for politically active Ugandans' willingness to punish corruption.
applications.industry_context: public sector governance / political economy research, Uganda
applications.ethical_note: An academic field/lab study of civic accountability mechanisms, not a persuasion technique aimed at end users -- illustrates the underlying loss-aversion mechanism in a governance context rather than a commercial application.

applications.title: A declining-stakes incentive to beat procrastination, designed with Dan Ariely's own advice
applications.description: Irrational Labs (Dan Ariely's applied-behavioral-design consultancy) describes a real personal incentive scheme: Kristen Berman (a named behavioral economist who works with Dan Ariely) had procrastinated on getting LASIK surgery for years. Her boyfriend Phil, after consulting Ariely directly, got several of Kristen's friends to pledge $500 total toward her surgery -- but structured as a decaying loss: she kept the full $500 only if she acted immediately, losing $100 on October 1st, $200 more on the 15th, and so on until the full amount was gone by November 26th, with a chart showing friends' photos and reactions at each deadline. The same post also reports a separate real workplace field experiment: employees pre-paid a bonus (who had to pay it back if they missed targets) outperformed normally-paid employees by 50% and 32% in two successive month-long trials, with no measured drop in satisfaction.
applications.industry_context: personal behavior change / interpersonal incentive design
applications.ethical_note: Dan Ariely himself directly addresses the ethical tension in the source article ('Think that using incentives is manipulation? Maybe.'), noting Kristen independently wanted the surgery and the scheme aimed at her own long-term benefit -- but it was designed and set in motion by others on her behalf without her initial input, a real asymmetry worth preserving honestly rather than smoothing into a simple 'user-beneficial' label.

applications.title: Apple reminding users what they'd lose by breaking their wind-down routine
applications.description: A proposed notification reminds a user, right as they're about to browse 'one last' video before bed, that continuing would mean losing the relaxed state they've already built during their wind-down period -- framing the choice around a loss already accrued rather than a future gain.
applications.ethical_note: This uses loss aversion in the user's own stated interest (protecting sleep they've already worked toward), not to extract money or engagement -- a clean, low-risk illustration in contrast with the Temu entry.

applications.title: Temu locking users into browsing to avoid forfeiting an unlocked prize
applications.description: Temu presents users with an apparent cash prize (e.g. a claimed £100) and restricts them to the product-selection page -- navigating away forfeits the accumulated coupons, exploiting reluctance to lose a prize the user believes they've already won to drive further, often impulsive, purchasing.
applications.ethical_note: The source's own language ('nudge us to make irrational spending decisions') names the intent directly -- a prize framed as already-won, then held hostage to navigation, is a deliberate loss-aversion trap rather than an incidental side effect, and belongs alongside this corpus's existing gambling-adjacent and dark-patterns literature.

applications.title: Typeform's long feature-loss list on its cancellation screen, reported as ineffective
applications.description: Typeform's cancellation flow displays an extensive list of features marked with X symbols that a user would lose by canceling -- intended to invoke loss aversion, but the source reports the approach backfired: users already knew what they'd lose, the list reminded them of paid features they weren't using, and its length created overload rather than persuasion.
applications.ethical_note: Not deceptive -- the listed features are real and genuinely lost -- but it is a deliberate attempt to trigger loss aversion at the exact moment a user is trying to leave, and its reported failure is itself useful evidence that this specific execution of the technique doesn't reliably work, worth pairing with the Temu entry's harder-edged version.

applications.title: Zapier's task-limit warning email, critiqued as under-using loss aversion
applications.description: Zapier's email warning users they're approaching their plan's task limit relies on text alone rather than a visual cue -- the source critiques this as underusing loss aversion, proposing an overfilled progress bar to make the impending loss feel more visceral than words convey.
applications.ethical_note: A genuine account-limit notification serving the user's own need to know before being cut off -- even the proposed, more visually urgent version would still be communicating a real, relevant fact rather than fabricating one.
